OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN rights chief warns of growing atrocity risk in Gaza, West Bank
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk warned Wednesday that Israeli actions and policies in Gaza and the occupied West Bank point to a growing risk of further atrocity crimes, and called on all states to act immediately. Türk said senior Israeli officials had repeatedly set out policies of annexation, ethnic cleansing and collective punishment in the West Bank, and cited incitement to violations that could amount to war crimes, crimes against humanity or genocide. The UN said nearly two million of Gaza’s 2.1 million residents have been forcibly displaced, often more than once, while most live in tents or makeshift shelters. Türk also cited the continuing destruction of civilian infrastructure, arbitrary detention and torture, and restrictions that deprive people of food, medicine and shelter. Türk called for independent investigations, accountability and support for international courts, while reminding Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups of their duties to protect civilians and humanitarian operations. He said unlawful killings continued despite the ceasefire announced in October 2025; Palestinian and Israeli tallies cited by RTÉ put the death toll since the truce at at least 1,600 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers.

items.title: [phys.org] Neolithic tomb pots point to fermented milk offerings in Denmark
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Researchers studying 330 Neolithic pots from western Zealand, Denmark, found corrosion on 31; 29 came from passage tombs. In experiments with reconstructed vessels, fresh, unpasteurized milk produced damage resembling the marks on ancient pottery, while beer and mead did not. The findings, published in Antiquity, suggest fermented dairy may have been placed with the dead, although corrosion alone cannot identify the contents with certainty. The results challenge an earlier interpretation that the corroded pots held beer, an idea based partly on evidence from brewing communities elsewhere. Fermentation makes milk more acidic, and the researchers say fermented dairy products could also have been easier to digest and lasted longer. Lead author Lone Claudi-Hansen, an archaeologist, said she hopes to examine pottery from other parts of Denmark to see whether the same pattern appears elsewhere.

The findings, published in Antiquity, suggest fermented dairy may have been placed with the dead, although corrosion alone cannot identify the contents with certainty (phys.org, science.org, discovermagazine.com, kristeligt-dagblad.dk). Where found: Only one of 143 pots from settlements showed the corrosion, and none of the pots recovered outside tomb entrances did (discovermagazine.com). Experimental side effect: During the 10-week trial, a white cheese briefly formed in the kefir pot (science.org). Selected vessels: The corroded tomb pots were among the finest in the sample and were nearly all decorated, which researchers say is consistent with deliberate selection (discovermagazine.com). Beer vessels: Two of the three experimental beer pots cracked at the neck, a failure distinct from the corrosion seen on the ancient pots (discovermagazine.com).

Where: West Zealand, Denmark
Perspective: Eva Rosenstock, an archaeologist at the University of Bonn, argued that a drink could carry prestige without being alcoholic. She said researchers should investigate unusual deposits and damage on pottery rather than dismiss them. (Science)
Perspective: Flemming Kaul, a senior researcher in archaeology at Denmark's National Museum, described passage tombs as gathering places that communities used across generations, a function tied to the shift from mobile hunting and gathering to settled farming. (Videnskab.dk)
Quote: "Particular foods and drinks could have had social or symbolic importance in funerary practices." (Lone Claudi-Hansen, archaeologist and study lead author, Phys.org)
Background: Farmers in Denmark began building passage tombs around 3300 B.C.E.; people buried their dead in and around these communal stone structures for almost 1,000 years (science.org).

🪶 ✏️

Researchers analyzing four fossil teeth from two caves in China’s Guangxi region identified Denisovan-related remains and evidence of a potentially distinct ancient human lineage, according to a study published in Nature on Nov. 25. The two Longchuandong teeth align with Denisovans, while two teeth from Chuanshandong—at least 100,800 years old—have traits that do not readily match any known East Asian Homo group. The findings suggest different archaic human populations lived in southern China during overlapping periods, but researchers cannot yet confidently assign the Chuanshandong teeth to a named group. Warm, humid conditions in the region hinder ancient DNA preservation, so researchers analyzed tooth shape and proteins. They say more fossils and molecular evidence are needed to establish the teeth’s evolutionary relationships.

items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Intense storms caused severe flooding in the U.S. Southwest and Florida in late October and early November, killing at least four people in the Southwest. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s seasonal outlook favors wetter conditions across much of the southern United States through February 2027 as a strong El Niño develops. Warm Pacific waters can increase atmospheric moisture, while recent rain left rivers high and soils saturated in parts of the Southwest, worsening runoff when further storms arrived. The winter’s snowpack remains uncertain; Colorado climatologist Russ Schumacher said rainfall could help the Colorado River’s reservoirs but would not reverse their decline.

items.title: [Macworld] Update: Microsoft offers explanation for day-long Internet outage
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Macworld

Whether you’re using a Mac, iPhone, or – shudder – a PC, a major Microsoft outage has disrupted Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services worldwide. The problems began on Thursday, November 12, and continued overnight into Friday, affecting businesses, schools and public services.

Microsoft said a server process had become overwhelmed, reducing capacity. Recovery proved difficult because some servers became unresponsive again as traffic returned. Features that depend on Exchange Online were particularly affected, although not every function within each Microsoft service stopped working.

A look at Downdetector and ThousandEyes Outages also showed complaints involving unrelated platforms. However, those reports don’t establish that every service was down or that they shared Microsoft’s underlying problem. Amazon told Macworld that AWS was operating normally. Some users also reported problems with iMessage, although Apple’s System Status page showed no corresponding outage at the time.

Microsoft reported signs of recovery as it restarted affected infrastructure and managed traffic, but had not provided a confirmed time for full restoration. The company had not established a final root cause and said there was no indication that malicious activity was responsible.

Settle in, and here’s hoping it’s fixed soon. You can track the Microsoft service health here, and we’ll keep this article updated as we learn more.

Update 4:17 am GMT / 11:17 pm ET: Final restoration confirmed

Microsoft confirmed that the Microsoft 365 outage had been resolved. The company claims the outage was caused by a technical problem associated with a network-capacity upgrade.

Recovery continues to be monitored.

Update 8:55 pm GMT / 3:55 pm ET: Network change blamed

Microsoft has apologized for the outage as it works to restore all systems to normal: “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”

Update 11:45 am GMT / 6.45 am ET: Recovery underway

Microsoft says it has completed recovery actions in Asia-Pacific and this recovery work is being extended to other regions, as per the Guardian’s live blog.

Update 10:15 am GMT / 5.15 am ET: The U.K. has woken up to the Microsoft outage

Microsoft’s service disruption continued into Friday, November 13, affecting Outlook email and Microsoft 365 features that depend on Exchange Online.

The disruption has affected NHS communications, with reports of NHS trusts, including Evelina London, a children’s healthcare provider, unable to send or receive emails.

Elsewhere, police forces have confirmed that some online reporting forms could be affected, but their ability to answer and respond to 999 and 101 calls had not been compromised.

Schools have also reported communication problems and asked parents to telephone rather than email their child’s school.

Microsoft’s Friday morning advisory, via the University of Pennsylvania’s Microsoft incident-report feed, says most core Teams calling, meetings and messaging functionality is unaffected, although calendar and other email-dependent features can fail.

Microsoft reported early signs of stabilization on Friday morning, but said capacity had not returned to normal and recovery remained uneven.

Update 9:45 pm ET: “Positive results”

Microsoft reported “seeing positive results” with its efforts to correct the outage as it restarted affected infrastructure and brought servers back into service in isolation.

Update 4:39 pm ET: AWS is normal

An Amazon spokesperson reached out to Macworld to let us know that AWS is functioning normally and has been all day.

Any disruptions today would have to be caused by something else.

Update 2:00 pm ET: The whole Internet is having major issues right now

Whether you’re using a Mac, iPhone, or – shudder – a PC, you may be having trouble accessing Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services.

Downdetector and ThousandEyes Outages are recording widespread reports of connectivity problems. Users have also reported issues with unrelated platforms, although those reports do not establish that every service is down or that they share the same underlying cause.

Some users are reporting problems with Apple services, including iMessage, but Apple’s System Status page shows no corresponding outage at the time of writing.

OpenAI and Anthropic have also reported disruption to the tools that connect their AI assistants to Microsoft 365. For ChatGPT users who connect Microsoft services, this could interrupt tasks that depend on retrieving information from those services.

The cause and expected restoration time remain unclear. We’ll update this live blog as providers confirm more information.

items.title: [Fast Company] DOJ sues Lyft for allegedly denying rides to people with disabilities
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The Justice Department has filed a lawsuit against Lyft, accusing the company of discriminating against passengers with disabilities who seek rides on its platform.

The federal lawsuit, filed Monday, says Lyft “is aware of, but fails to prevent and remedy” several discriminatory practices against riders who need accommodations under the Americans With Disabilities Act. That includes denying rides to people who have service animals or use stowable wheelchairs and refusing to let passengers with mobility issues sit in the front seat, the suit alleges.

“Individuals with disabilities should be able to rely on ride-share services free of discrimination,” said Jesus A. Osete, acting assistant attorney general, in a statement. “We intend to uphold the ADA’s promise that people with disabilities are entitled to equal access in every part of public life, including essential transportation services.”

Lyft firmly rejected the accusations in a statement.

The lawsuit is the latest from the federal government that targets ride-hailing companies for the treatment of would-be riders with disabilities. The administration filed a similar lawsuit against Uber last year, which is ongoing. Uber settled a separate suit in 2022, and Lyft settled a different one in 2020. The companies stress that their policies and in-app tools require that drivers provide ADA accommodations and remind them of the consequences of refusing to do so.

The new lawsuit against Lyft named several examples of people across the country who hailed a ride on the platform but had one—or, in some cases, several—drivers refuse to take them to their destination, including as recently as last month. Those individuals experienced delays in getting to medical appointments, cancellation fees, and other issues as a result, the suit said.

Lyft policies require drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or mobility devices, and “drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation,” the company said in a statement.

“We’ve cooperated with the DOJ throughout its review and remain committed to serving every rider, including riders with disabilities,” the company said.

The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The Department of Justice said it is seeking $53 million for individuals who have been discriminated against and have submitted complaints to Lyft or the department.

—By Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press

items.title: [Macworld] How accurately does the Apple Watch measure your heart rate? We put it to the test
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Macworld

With the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, Apple introduced a new health-sensing system. The new energy-efficient LED sensors measure heart rate every five seconds. Heart rate variability is also measured significantly more frequently than before. Macwelt was able to verify this in our review of the Apple Watch Series 12. The watch now measures your pulse every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, and heart rate variability is now recorded every five minutes. The battery still lasts for 24 hours.

This is exciting, because the Apple Watch already had stellar heart-rate tracking. How often and how accurately has the Apple Watch been measuring key health parameters to date? Apple hides the answers to these questions in its support documents. For some measurements, there are no official figures at all. So we took a closer look using the Apple Watch Series 11, which has the same third-gen optical heart rate sensor that was introduced with the Apple Watch Series 6.

How often does the Apple Watch Series 11 measure heart rate?

The answer to this question depends on the situation and the settings on your Apple Watch. In workout mode, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate every five seconds. The watch also measures your heart rate at this high frequency for the first three minutes after your workout. However, there is also a special setting for long workouts, where the user can activate power-saving mode if required. Apple claims that measurements are taken less frequently in this mode. I recorded a HIIT workout using the Polar H10 chest strap as a reference device. I also started the same workout on the Apple Watch Series 11.

Foundry

The Apple Watch actually measures heart rate every five seconds while the wearer is exercising. Measurements in power-saving mode during a workout also take place every five seconds. However, the system pauses the measurement for several minutes. This means that the heart rate is measured in short intervals every 5 seconds, then the Apple Watch pauses. You can see this on the graph of the heart rates measured during the workout up to the green line: up to that point, the Apple Watch was running in power-saving mode; after that, I switched it off.

Speaking of power-saving mode. If this mode is activated all the time, no background measurements take place, neither of the heart rate nor of heart rate variability. Furthermore, the vital signs data following a recorded night’s sleep lacks the oxygen saturation readings from during the night.

The Apple Watch can also measure your heart rate every second, just like chest straps do during a workout. However, these measurements only occur sporadically: during user-initiated ECG readings and during background HRV measurements. When you launch the ECG app and place your finger on the Digital Crown, the animation on the Watch and the PDF generated afterwards show the heart rate readings for every second. During HRV measurement, too, the Apple Watch records each heart rate over the course of a minute and then uses a specific formula to calculate the time interval between individual heartbeats.

In the background, and particularly at night while you’re asleep, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate every five minutes. However, the measurements aren’t as regular as they are during exercise. The intervals can vary more significantly when you’re at rest.

I exported and analysed measurements from a sample night using the Health app. For the sake of clarity, the chart above shows only one hour. During six and a half hours of sleep, the Apple Watch took 83 measurements. The average interval between measurements here is 4 minutes 39 seconds, although gaps of 16 minutes or as little as 40 seconds are also possible.

How accurately does the Apple Watch measure heart rate data?

When unveiling the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple claimed that the new smartwatch was the most accurate heart rate fitness tracker on the market. While we can only verify this claim through a single test, older models show that the Apple Watch was already quite accurate when it came to heart rate measurement.

When we tested the Apple Watch Ultra 3, we found that the Ultra’s readings deviated only very slightly from those of the chest strap. I analysed the same HIIT workout described above using the Apple Watch Series 11. The following picture emerges from the progression of the two graphs. On average, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate quite accurately during exercise.

The correlation coefficient between the two measurements–from the Polar H10 and the Apple Watch Series 11–is 0.95. This means the Apple Watch measures quite closely to a chest strap. On average, the two readings differ by just one beat. However, there are outliers: the higher the heart rate, the less accurate the measurement becomes. This can be seen in the line showing heart rates of 160 beats per minute and above. The measurement is also rather inaccurate in power-saving mode, as the Apple Watch can completely miss heart rate spikes due to the sporadic mode.

The new features Apple announced for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are exciting because they effectively turn the entire heart rate measurement algorithm on its head.

items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Children and young adults with atopic dermatitis had 28% higher odds of sleep disturbance than peers without the condition, a retrospective review of 26,395 patients at an urban primary care clinic found. The association remained after researchers accounted for coexisting atopy and mental health conditions; neither significantly changed the link. The study included patients aged 0 to 21; 14.5% had atopic dermatitis and 10.3% had sleep disturbance. Samantha Sundermeier, DO, an attending physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, said future studies should assess disease severity, treatment response and sleep over time using validated measures and patient-reported outcomes.

items.title: [news.mit.edu] Older adults show weaker brain-clearing fluid waves during sleep
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

MIT researchers found that older adults had significantly weaker waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which helps clear waste from the brain during sleep, than younger adults. The researchers used brain imaging and electroencephalography to study volunteers ages 18 to 39 and 60 to 84, linking the reduced flow partly to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and diminished vascular responses. Separately, a study described in a paper shared on Reddit found that LSD-related gene-expression patterns in rats and mice ran counter to some patterns associated with human brain aging. LSD also reduced certain amyloid-beta-related changes in mouse brain-cell cultures. These are preclinical findings, not evidence that LSD prevents dementia in people.

items.title: [theguardian.com] Anthropic mathematician's Claude-assisted Riemann claim prompts math departments to adapt
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says the company’s Claude assistant helped him prove the Riemann hypothesis, a longstanding mathematical claim about prime-number distribution. The claimed proof remains subject to human verification. Johns Hopkins University’s mathematics department has issued guidance for Ph.D. applicants and job candidates, saying it expects transparency about AI use and will not give written work positive weight unless candidates demonstrate they understand it. Professor Yiannis Sakellaridis said the guidance was prompted by the risk that candidates could submit AI-generated proofs without learning the underlying mathematics, not by a specific applicant case. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei rejected the idea that people should hand governance to AI, while David Krueger, founder of the nonprofit Evitable, argued that concern about losing control calls for a halt to advanced AI development. Researchers and technology leaders have debated whether the mathematical advances signal progress toward systems that exceed human capabilities.

items.title: [datacenternews.asia] IEC launches standards programme for broader data-centre sustainability assessment
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), a global standards body, has launched a programme to develop international standards for assessing data centres using measures beyond their direct electricity and water use. Its proposed “Total Contribution” framework would weigh environmental costs against effects on power grids, regional economies and public services as demand for cloud computing and artificial-intelligence workloads grows. The framework covers energy and grid integration, environmental stewardship, economic and digital productivity, and societal resilience. A new IEC standards group will develop common metrics, reporting protocols and assurance methods for the IT and utility sectors. The group will examine options including demand response, renewable generation and water-saving cooling.
